summary:
AstroVita is a browser-based astronaut health exploration prototype developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. It brings spaceflight health context to life through an interactive 3D anatomy view, where users can explore the heart, lungs, brain, skeleton, and immune system. The dashboard also demonstrates crew profiles, simulated mission scenarios, optional self-reported check-ins, 14-day history views, and CSV export.

Because the official challenge resources provide research context rather than a connected astronaut telemetry dataset, AstroVita clearly separates NASA-linked information from synthetic demonstrations and user-entered values. It does not present mock readings as NASA data or offer diagnoses and unvalidated medical thresholds.

This matters because crews on long-duration missions need clear ways to understand and review health information, especially when far from Earth. AstroVita demonstrates how thoughtful visualization and transparent data boundaries can make a health-monitoring workflow engaging without overstating what the available evidence supports.
details:
AstroVita is a browser-based prototype developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. It helps users explore astronaut health through an interactive 3D anatomy dashboard focused on the heart, lungs, brain, skeleton, and immune system. Users can select a body-system marker to view relevant NASA Human Research Program context, switch between three fictional crew profiles and four scripted scenarios, enter optional health check-ins, review a 14-day history, and export their entries as a CSV file.

The project’s key benefit is making a complex topic easier to explore while clearly distinguishing source-based context, simulated demonstration values, and user-entered information. The official challenge resources reviewed provide research context, but no astronaut telemetry dataset or live sensor feed. AstroVita therefore does not present demo values as NASA data, diagnose conditions, or set medical thresholds. Check-ins stay in the user’s browser and are not sent to a server.

The intended impact is educational: to demonstrate how a clear, interactive health-information workflow could support exploration during space missions, while showing what would need real data and qualified medical review before any clinical use. The project was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, Tailwind CSS, Wouter, Recharts, React Hook Form, and Zod. It requires no special hardware, only a modern web browser.

Creatively, the human body itself becomes the main navigation interface. The team considered the constraints of long-duration missions, usability, data provenance, privacy, accurate health interpretation, model licensing, and fallback behavior if 3D rendering is unavailable. All anatomy visuals are educational assets, not astronaut scans or NASA data.
